paragraphs: Finding out that pests have been living above your ceiling can leave you with an uneasy feeling, even after the scratching stops. What is still up there? Has the insulation been affected? And how do you know when the job is really finished?

Getting the animals out matters, but it does not remove what they left behind. When droppings, urine, nests, or other contamination have reached the insulation, a full attic remediation brings the next steps together: removing the old material, cleaning the attic, closing entry points, and preparing the space for fresh insulation.
You do not have to figure out every part on your own. Start by finding out what happened in the attic. From there, the work can be planned in an order that makes sense.

sections.heading: The Attic Can Be Quiet Without Being Restored
sections.markdown:
It is a relief when the noises stop. Pest control deals with the animals that are present. Attic restoration deals with the space they leave behind.

Depending on the animal, the attic may still contain droppings, nesting material, guano, urine-stained insulation, lingering odor, or damaged material. Insulation may also have been pulled apart, flattened, or moved away from the areas it should cover.

sections.heading: First, Find Out What Actually Reached the Insulation
sections.markdown:
A mouse in the kitchen, a single bat indoors, or a roofline gap does not automatically prove the insulation is contaminated. An inspection should connect the evidence to the material itself.

Droppings, urine, nests, or guano mixed into the insulation tell a different story from ordinary dust. Chewed wiring or damaged ducts can show pest activity, but they need their own evaluation and do not prove the insulation is contaminated by themselves.

Photos and an explanation of what was found should help you understand the recommendation. You should not have to climb into a dirty attic or disturb waste to get answers. [CDC advises against sweeping or vacuuming rodent waste before it has been properly disinfected](https://www.cdc.gov/healthy-pets/rodent-control/clean-up.html).

sections.heading: Why a Full Reset Can Be Better Than Covering the Problem
sections.markdown:
Adding insulation can improve coverage. It cannot remove droppings, urine, nests, or odor sources underneath it. Spraying a treatment over old insulation is not the same as taking contaminated material out, either.

Spot cleaning can leave an easy-to-reach area looking better while other parts remain hidden. Removing the existing insulation gives the crew access to the attic floor, including places that were difficult to inspect or clean before. It also creates an opportunity to address air leaks and prepare the attic before new insulation goes in.

That is the practical case for full remediation: deal with the aftermath and the preparation together, rather than placing a new layer over unanswered questions.

Not every attic cleanup is a pest-remediation project. Clean, dry insulation may still be worth keeping when the issue is ordinary debris or low insulation depth. A roof leak or damaged material can also lead to restoration for a different reason. The [removal-versus-top-off guide](/resources/insulation-removal-vs-top-off/) explains that broader decision.

sections.heading: Different Animals Need Different First Steps
sections.markdown:
### Mice

A pest professional can address active mice and assess how they are getting in. The insulation work then focuses on what they left behind. Read [Does Attic Insulation Need to Be Removed After Mice?](/resources/attic-insulation-removal-after-mice/).

### Bats

Bats need a wildlife professional to plan exclusion around the colony, the season, and local requirements. Closing an opening at the wrong time can trap animals inside, including young bats that cannot yet fly. Our [bat-guano guide](/resources/bat-guano-attic-insulation-removal/) explains how exclusion and attic restoration fit together. If a bat was found indoors, contact animal control or your health department before handling or releasing it; [CDC explains the next steps](https://www.cdc.gov/rabies/prevention/bats.html).

### Squirrels, raccoons, birds, and other wildlife

The animal, any active nest, and the condition of the waste all affect the first steps. Raccoon waste and accumulated bat or bird droppings need particular care. A wildlife or cleanup specialist may need to lead that work before the insulation is removed and replaced.

sections.heading: Cleanup Handles What Happened. Exclusion Addresses How It Happened.
sections.markdown:
These are two parts of the same recovery, but they are not interchangeable. Cleaning the attic does not close the opening an animal used. Closing the opening does not remove contaminated insulation.

Pest exclusion focuses on outside entry points around rooflines, soffits, vents, siding, and utility penetrations. The right repair needs to keep animals out without blocking ventilation the attic is supposed to have. Active exits must be handled in the order established by the pest or wildlife professional.

Attic air sealing is different. It closes gaps between the living space and the attic around pipes, wiring, wall tops, and the attic hatch. That work is easier to reach before fresh insulation covers the attic floor.

Fresh insulation finishes the restoration; it does not replace entry-point repairs or ongoing pest care. Exterior materials can age and new gaps can develop, so maintenance still matters after the project is complete.

sections.heading: What Full Attic Remediation Looks Like
sections.markdown:
Here is how the work comes together.

1. **Address the active pest problem.** The pest or wildlife professional determines the appropriate control or exclusion plan before the attic is rebuilt.
2. **Protect the home and remove the old insulation.** The attic access and removal route are protected. Existing insulation and pest debris are taken out using methods suited to the material and contamination.
3. **Clean and inspect the exposed attic.** With the insulation out, the crew can see what was hidden. Debris removal, cleaning, and the appropriate sanitation or odor treatment happen before anything is covered again.
4. **Close entry points and prepare the space.** This can include coordinated exclusion, air sealing, baffles, attic dams, hatch improvements, and protection around recessed lights. Electrical, structural, or other repairs are handled by the right professional.
5. **Install fresh insulation and review the result.** New insulation goes over a prepared attic. Completion photos and a walkthrough of the work help you understand what changed and what to keep an eye on afterward.

The order can change when another trade needs access, but fresh insulation should come after the attic is prepared.

sections.heading: Some Problems Need More Than One Professional
sections.markdown:
An attic can have more than one issue at a time. A roof leak, damaged wire, duct problem, or unsafe framing may need attention alongside the pest cleanup. You should be told who will handle each part and how the work fits together.

The cleanup method matters, too. [NIOSH recommends controlling dust when bat or bird droppings are disturbed](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/histoplasmosis/prevention/elimination-and-engineering-controls.html), and [CDC provides separate precautions for raccoon waste](https://www.cdc.gov/baylisascaris/prevention/index.html). A routine spray treatment should not be presented as a solution for every kind of contamination.

If the attic may contain vermiculite, leave it alone until you have qualified advice. [EPA recommends leaving vermiculite undisturbed](https://www.epa.gov/asbestos/my-attic-has-vermiculite-insulation-it-am-i-risk-should-i-take-it-out) because it may contain asbestos. That is not a material to remove with ordinary insulation equipment.

sections.heading: Why Good Attic Recommends Starting Fresh After Pest Contamination
sections.markdown:
Once pest contamination is confirmed in attic insulation, Good Attic recommends removing the existing insulation and completing a full attic remediation. We do not recommend covering contaminated material or treating only the easiest visible area as the finished solution.

For us, the value of starting fresh is being able to see and address what was underneath. We remove the old insulation, clean and prepare the attic, address attic-related entry points and air leaks, and install fresh borate-treated blown-in cellulose. We work hand in hand with pest, wildlife, cleanup, and other professionals when their expertise is needed.

We inspect the attic, share what we find, and build the quote with you onsite. Attic size, access, cleanup, and repairs help shape the price. Progress and completion photos show how the work comes together. You should be able to move forward with a clear plan—not feel pressured into a decision you do not understand.

sections.heading: One Mouse Does Not Automatically Mean the Insulation Is Contaminated
sections.markdown:
The decision should be based on what is actually found in and around the insulation.

### Card 1 — Signs the insulation has been affected

Droppings in or through the insulation, urine staining, nesting material, mouse remains, persistent pest odor, and insulation that has been shredded, tunneled, flattened, or displaced all point toward contamination or damage within the attic material.

### Card 2 — Signs that need a closer look

Chewed wiring, damaged ducts, gnawed storage boxes, or an opening along the roofline can show that mice have been present. Those clues matter, but they do not prove by themselves that the insulation has been contaminated.

### Card 3 — Dark insulation may mean something else

Insulation can turn dark or gray where household air has been leaking through gaps in the attic floor and carrying dust with it. That may point to an air-sealing problem rather than mice.

**Safety note:** Do not stir up dry droppings or nesting material for a closer look. CDC guidance recommends wetting and disinfecting rodent waste before it is handled rather than sweeping or vacuuming it while dry.

sections.heading: Why One Visible Area May Not Tell the Whole Story
sections.markdown:
The attic hatch is usually the easiest place to see. It is not necessarily the only place mice traveled.

Mice can move along framing, wiring, plumbing, and ductwork. They may tunnel through loose-fill insulation or build nests in low, protected areas that are difficult to see from the opening.

One clue does not prove the entire attic is contaminated. It does mean the rest of the space should be inspected before anyone adds insulation or treats only that one spot. The goal is not to make the problem sound larger than it is. The goal is to understand it well enough to solve it once.

---

sections.heading: Why New Insulation or Spot Cleaning Is Not a Complete Fix
sections.markdown:
Fresh insulation can improve depth, but it cannot remove droppings, urine, nests, odor, or damaged material underneath it. It may also make the attic floor harder to inspect and clean later.

Spot cleaning has the same limitation. It can make one easy-to-reach area look better while leaving contaminated insulation elsewhere.

Once contamination is confirmed in the insulation, a full remediation gives the attic a true reset: the old material comes out, the attic floor is exposed, the space can be cleaned and prepared, and fresh insulation goes back over a better starting point.

For the broader keep-or-remove question, see [Insulation Removal vs. Top-Off](https://goodattic.energy/resources/insulation-removal-vs-top-off/).

---

sections.heading: Mouse Control Comes First; Attic Remediation Handles What Was Left Behind
sections.markdown:
A pest professional should address active mice before attic restoration begins. That work deals with the animals that are still present.

Attic remediation deals with the insulation, droppings, nests, odor, damaged areas, and entry points left behind. The order matters: active mice can disturb new insulation and reuse openings before the attic has a chance to be restored.

---

sections.heading: What Full Attic Remediation Usually Involves
sections.markdown:
### Step 1 — Handle the active mouse problem

A pest professional addresses the mice that are currently present.

### Step 2 — Protect the home and removal path

The attic access and the hose route leading outside are covered and prepared before old insulation comes out.

### Step 3 — Remove the existing insulation and pest debris

The old insulation, droppings, nests, and other debris come out instead of being covered. Commercial insulation-removal equipment moves loose material through a hose to exterior removal bags.

### Step 4 — Expose, clean, and inspect the attic floor

With the insulation out, the crew can see what was hidden, remove remaining debris, and complete the sanitation and odor treatment needed for the project.

### Step 5 — Close entry points and prepare the attic

This can include pest exclusion, attic-floor air sealing, baffles, attic dams, hatch improvements, weatherstripping, and protective covers around applicable recessed lights.

### Step 6 — Install fresh insulation and document the work

Fresh borate-treated blown-in cellulose can be installed after the attic is clean and prepared. Progress and completion photos show how the space changed from start to finish.

---

sections.heading: Cleaning the Attic and Closing Mouse Entry Points
sections.markdown:
Removing contaminated insulation handles what the mice left behind. Exclusion work addresses how they entered.

Attic-related openings can appear around rooflines, soffits, vents, siding transitions, and utility penetrations. Closing those openings can reduce the chance of another problem.

Pest exclusion and attic air sealing solve different problems. Exclusion closes openings mice use to enter from outside. Air sealing closes gaps between the living space and the attic around wiring, pipes, top plates, chases, fixtures, and the attic hatch. Both may be part of a full remediation.

Fresh borate-treated cellulose can add a pest-deterrent benefit after cleanup. It does not make the attic permanently pest-proof, so exterior maintenance and continued pest monitoring still matter.

---

sections.heading: Some Attics Need a Different Expert Before Restoration Can Continue
sections.markdown:
Suspected vermiculite, unsafe framing, fire damage, electrical damage, or contamination involving HVAC equipment may require another qualified professional.

If the attic may contain vermiculite, do not disturb it like ordinary insulation. EPA advises homeowners to assume it may contain asbestos and to use a qualified asbestos professional when removal is necessary.

---

sections.heading: What Changes the Cost of Mouse-Damaged Attic Remediation?
sections.markdown:
The price depends on how much material needs to come out, how difficult the attic is to access, what the mice left behind, and what it will take to clean, seal, and rebuild the space.

Common cost factors include attic size, insulation depth, access, the amount of pest debris, home and hose-path protection, cleanup and odor treatment, entry-point work, air sealing, attic preparation, replacement-insulation depth, and any specialist work the attic requires.

A useful quote should make the sequence clear so the homeowner understands what is coming out, what is being cleaned or sealed, and what is going back into the attic.

---

sections.heading: When Mouse Contamination Is Confirmed, We Believe in Starting Fresh
sections.markdown:
Once mouse contamination is confirmed in the insulation, Good Attic recommends removing the existing insulation and completing a full attic remediation. We do not believe in covering contaminated material with new insulation or treating only one visible area as the finished solution.

Good Attic can coordinate active pest control when needed, protect the access and hose path, remove loose-fill insulation through commercial equipment into exterior bags, complete the cleanup and attic preparation, address attic-related entry points, and rebuild the space with borate-treated cellulose.

Government guidance helps explain how rodent waste should be handled safely. The recommendation to complete full remediation is Good Attic’s professional standard for restoring a mouse-contaminated attic.

---

paragraphs: Discovering a bat in the house or finding guano in the attic can be alarming. It does not automatically mean the entire attic is ruined, and it does not mean the first step is tearing everything out. There is a clear order that protects the people in the home, respects the bats, and keeps the attic work from being done twice.

First, determine whether bats are still using the structure and let a qualified wildlife professional plan the exclusion at the right time. Then inspect where the guano, urine, and roosting debris actually reached.

One bat does not automatically mean the insulation needs to be removed. The question changes when guano or urine has reached the insulation, contamination has collected beneath an active roost, or the insulation itself carries odor or visible damage tied to bat activity.

sections.heading: A Bat Sighting Is Not the Same as Contaminated Insulation
sections.markdown:
Seeing a bat outdoors does not suggest an attic problem by itself. A bat found inside, repeated activity around the roofline at dusk, guano below an opening, or evidence of an attic roost is a reason to look more closely.

### Card 1 — A single bat

A lone bat can enter through an open door, window, chimney, or small gap. One indoor bat does not automatically mean a colony is living in the attic.

### Card 2 — An established roost

Repeated evening activity, regular sounds from the same area, staining around an opening, or guano collecting beneath a roofline gap can suggest that bats are using the structure more consistently.

### Card 3 — Contamination in the insulation

Insulation contamination means guano, urine, or roosting debris has reached or mixed into the insulation—or the insulation itself carries odor or visible damage tied to the roost. Guano limited to a separate hard surface may present a different cleanup question and does not automatically mean all of the insulation needs to be removed.

**Health and safety note:** Do not handle a bat with bare hands. If physical contact may have occurred—or a bat was found in a room with someone who may not have noticed contact—contact the local health department and do not release the bat until you receive guidance.

---

sections.heading: Bat Exclusion Comes Before Attic Restoration
sections.markdown:
When bats are still using an attic, the first job is getting them out safely and at the proper time.

A wildlife professional should identify the active exits and determine when exclusion can happen. One-way devices or another appropriate method can allow bats to leave without letting them back in. The openings should not be permanently sealed too early.

Timing matters because young bats may not yet be able to fly. Excluding adults while pups remain inside can create an animal-welfare problem and may push bats toward other openings into the home. Utah, Missouri, and Kansas each provide their own guidance, so the wildlife professional should set the plan for the location and season.

---

sections.heading: A Clear Sequence for a Bat-Affected Attic
sections.markdown:
### Step 1 — Evaluate the active colony

A qualified wildlife professional identifies the exits and determines whether young bats or seasonal rules affect the timing.

### Step 2 — Let the bats leave

One-way exclusion or another appropriate method allows the bats to leave. Active exits remain available until the wildlife professional confirms the sequence is complete.

### Step 3 — Coordinate permanent closure

Once the bats are out, the openings they used can be sealed in the right order. Other gaps around the roofline, vents, soffits, siding, chimneys, and penetrations can also be reviewed.

### Step 4 — Evaluate the guano and insulation

The attic is inspected to determine whether guano or urine reached the insulation, whether odor remains, and whether the cleanup needs a specialized provider.

### Step 5 — Remove contaminated insulation and clean the attic

When contamination has reached the insulation, the existing material and guano-related debris can be removed so the attic can be cleaned and prepared instead of covered.

### Step 6 — Rebuild the insulation layer

After the wildlife and cleanup work is complete, the attic can be air sealed, prepared, and insulated with fresh material.

---

sections.heading: The Amount and Condition of the Guano Help Determine Who Should Lead the Cleanup
sections.markdown:
A small amount of guano on an open hard surface is different from years of dry accumulation mixed into loose-fill insulation.

Bat droppings can create dust when disturbed. NIOSH advises against dry sweeping or shoveling and describes dust-control and high-efficiency vacuum methods for professional cleanup. Large, dusty, difficult-to-contain, or otherwise specialized conditions may need a company equipped to lead that level of work.

A homeowner should not climb into a dusty roost and begin sweeping, shoveling, or moving insulation. The attic should be evaluated before the material is disturbed.

---

sections.heading: When Guano Reaches the Insulation, Covering It Is Not a Reset
sections.markdown:
New insulation can add depth, but it cannot remove guano, urine, odor, roosting debris, or damaged material underneath it.

Once contamination in the insulation is established and the wildlife sequence is ready, the existing insulation and guano-related debris can be removed so the attic can be cleaned and prepared.

A full remediation may include home protection, insulation removal, guano-related cleanup, odor or sanitation treatment, attic-floor inspection, coordinated entry-point closure, air sealing, ventilation preparation, fresh insulation, and completion photos.

The goal is not simply to make one visible pile disappear. It is to give the attic a clean starting point after the active bat problem has been handled.

---

sections.heading: Bat Entry Points Must Be Closed in the Right Sequence
sections.markdown:
Bat exclusion and attic restoration overlap, but they are not the same job.

The wildlife professional manages the active colony and determines when one-way exclusion and permanent closure can happen. The attic-restoration team can then coordinate insulation removal, cleanup, preparation, and entry-point work around that plan.

Common access points may include roofline gaps, unscreened vents, openings under eaves, loose siding or trim, chimney transitions, and spaces around pipes or wiring.

Closing those openings can reduce the chance of bats returning, but new gaps may develop as exterior materials age. Continued maintenance still matters.

---

sections.heading: What Changes the Cost of a Bat-Affected Attic Project?
sections.markdown:
The price depends on the attic size, the amount and location of the guano, whether the insulation has been contaminated, how difficult the cleanup is, and what the attic needs before fresh insulation can be installed.

Other factors may include wildlife exclusion, entry-point repairs, access and headroom, odor or sanitation treatment, air sealing, baffles, replacement-insulation depth, and work led by a specialized cleanup provider.

The clearest proposal separates the wildlife work, specialized cleanup, attic restoration, and replacement insulation so the homeowner knows who is handling each part.

paragraphs: Water in the attic can make every decision feel urgent. Is the roof still leaking? Is the insulation ruined? Is there mold? Can the material dry, or does it need to come out?

Start with the source of the moisture. Fix that problem, then inspect the insulation and the materials around it. A small damp area discovered quickly may have a different answer than insulation that is soaked, matted, smelly, contaminated, or visibly damaged.

Wet insulation should not be covered with fresh material while the source is still active or the attic is still holding moisture. Once the cause and the extent are understood, the next step becomes much clearer.

sections.heading: Fix the Water Problem Before Deciding What Insulation Can Stay
sections.markdown:
Insulation is often where a moisture problem becomes visible, but it is rarely where the problem begins.

### Card 1 — Roof or flashing leaks

Water can enter around shingles, flashing, valleys, vents, chimneys, skylights, or roof penetrations. It may travel along framing before it reaches the insulation.

### Card 2 — Plumbing, HVAC, or condensate problems

A plumbing leak, sweating duct, clogged condensate line, overflowing drain pan, or problem around attic equipment can wet insulation from inside the attic.

### Card 3 — Condensation or exhaust air

Warm, moist household air can reach cold attic surfaces through air leaks. Bathroom or dryer exhaust that ends in the attic can also add moisture where it does not belong.

Adding insulation before the source is corrected can hide the evidence and set up the same problem again. Depending on the cause, a roofer, plumber, HVAC contractor, or another specialist may need to make the repair first.

---

sections.heading: A Damp Corner Is Different From a Soaked or Contaminated Attic
sections.markdown:
A small area that became damp recently from a clean-water leak may be evaluated after the source is repaired and the surrounding materials are checked. Insulation that is saturated, matted, smelly, contaminated, visibly damaged, or left wet for an extended period is much more likely to need removal.

| What the inspection finds | Likely direction |
|---|---|
| A small, recently damp area with the source corrected | Inspect the insulation and nearby materials before deciding what can remain |
| Insulation that is soaked, matted, clumped, compressed, or uneven | Removal and replacement are more likely |
| Strong odor, visible growth, dirty water, or pest contamination | Bring in the appropriate professional and plan for removal of damaged materials |
| Wet decking, framing, drywall, ducts, wiring, or equipment | Correct and evaluate those materials before rebuilding the attic |
| Suspected vermiculite | Stop ordinary disturbance and involve a qualified asbestos professional |

The goal is not to save insulation at any cost or remove more than necessary. It is to leave the attic dry, clean, and ready for whatever comes next.

---

sections.heading: Wet Cellulose and Wet Fiberglass Can Behave Differently
sections.markdown:
### Cellulose

Loose-fill cellulose can absorb water, clump, settle, and lose the even coverage it had before the leak. Saturated, smelly, contaminated, or badly matted cellulose is a poor base for another layer.

### Fiberglass

Fiberglass does not absorb water in exactly the same way, but wet material can still hold moisture against wood, drywall, paper facing, dust, and debris. It should not be kept simply because the surface feels dry. Its shape, cleanliness, odor, and the condition of the materials around it still matter.

### The label is not the whole answer

How long the insulation was wet, whether the water was clean, how far it traveled, and what happened to the roof deck or ceiling below matter more than a simple material rule.

---

sections.heading: The Materials Around It May Need Attention Too
sections.markdown:
Water may affect roof decking, framing, ceiling drywall, ducts, HVAC equipment, wiring, fixtures, baffles, and soffit areas. A ceiling stain may be the first clue, but it does not always show the full water path.

Looking at the insulation alone cannot tell you whether another part of the attic also needs attention. An inspection helps follow the moisture and identify which professional should handle each part.

---

sections.heading: Some Insulation Can Be Evaluated; Some Is Better Removed
sections.markdown:
Removal is more likely when the insulation is soaked, matted, smelly, contaminated, visibly damaged, or preventing the materials underneath from being inspected.

It may also make sense when the material has lost its shape, water traveled through a large area, pest waste is mixed into it, the attic floor needs to be exposed for cleanup or air sealing, or nearby decking, ceiling, ducts, or wiring need attention.

A limited damp area found quickly may have a different answer. The important thing is not to close the attic back up before the source, the insulation, and the nearby materials have been properly evaluated.

---

sections.heading: Repair First, Then Remove, Prepare, and Rebuild
sections.markdown:
1. **Stop the moisture source.** Repair the roof leak, plumbing issue, condensate problem, exhaust problem, or other cause.
2. **See how far the water traveled.** Inspect the insulation and the roof deck, framing, ceiling, ducts, wiring, and equipment that can be seen.
3. **Bring in the right professional.** Roofing, plumbing, HVAC, electrical, mold, structural, or water-restoration work may need to happen first.
4. **Remove material that should not remain.** Take out insulation that is saturated, matted, smelly, contaminated, or too damaged to provide a good starting point.
5. **Prepare the exposed attic.** Complete the cleanup, air sealing, baffles, ventilation preparation, and other attic work needed before insulation goes back in.
6. **Install fresh insulation when the attic is ready.** The new material should be the final layer over a dry, repaired, properly prepared space.

---

sections.heading: Wet Insulation With Pest Contamination Needs a More Complete Reset
sections.markdown:

paragraphs: Replacing a roof is already a major project, so it is understandable not to want another surprise waiting underneath it. The good news is that new roofing does not automatically mean the attic insulation has to be replaced.

A roof replacement is, however, one of the best times to look at the attic and make an informed decision. If the old roof leaked, pests entered around the roofline, the insulation is wet or contaminated, or the attic needs air sealing and ventilation work, coordinating the projects can prevent a second major disruption later.
The answer depends on the condition of the insulation and what the roofing work will expose—not simply on the age of the shingles.

sections.heading: What the Attic Inspection Finds Should Guide the Next Step
sections.markdown:
| What the inspection finds | Likely direction |
|---|---|
| Insulation is clean, dry, pest-free, and evenly distributed | It may be able to remain |
| Insulation is thin but otherwise usable | Prepare the attic and consider a top-off |
| Insulation is wet, matted, smelly, or damaged by a roof leak | Correct the leak and evaluate removal and replacement |
| Mice or bats contaminated the insulation | Handle the active pest issue, then complete full attic remediation |
| Broad air sealing, decking, baffle, or ventilation work is needed | Coordinate the roofing and attic projects before either crew begins |
| Suspected vermiculite is present | Stop ordinary disturbance and involve a qualified asbestos professional |

A roof replacement does not automatically mean the insulation must be replaced. But when the attic already needs removal, cleanup, air sealing, pest exclusion, or ventilation preparation, coordinating the work with the roof project is usually smarter than finishing one project and reopening the same areas later.

---

sections.heading: Clean, Dry Insulation May Not Need to Be Replaced With the Roof
sections.markdown:
If the attic insulation is dry, clean, pest-free, evenly distributed, and still providing useful coverage, there may be no reason to remove it simply because the roof is being replaced.

The attic may still benefit from smaller improvements, such as:

- Adding insulation where the existing depth is low
- Air sealing before a new top layer is installed
- Installing or repairing baffles near soffit vents
- Improving the attic hatch
- Correcting insulation that has been disturbed or compressed

Keeping usable insulation can be the right answer. The important thing is to inspect it before the roofing work hides clues about leaks, decking damage, or pest entry.

For a deeper comparison, see [Insulation Removal vs. Top-Off](https://goodattic.energy/resources/insulation-removal-vs-top-off/).

---

sections.heading: Old Insulation Should Come Out When It Is Part of the Problem
sections.markdown:
Replacing the insulation becomes a stronger choice when the old material is wet, smelly, pest-contaminated, heavily compressed, badly disturbed, or blocking access to work that needs to happen underneath it.

Removal may make sense when:

- A roof leak soaked or matted the insulation
- Water traveled across a wider area than the ceiling stain suggests
- Mice, bats, or other animals contaminated the material
- Droppings, nesting debris, guano, or persistent odor remain
- The attic floor needs to be exposed for air sealing or cleanup
- Decking, wiring, ducts, or other materials beneath the insulation need attention
- The existing insulation is no longer a good base for a top-off

The goal is not to add attic work to every roofing project. It is to avoid installing a new roof over an attic problem that will still need to be opened, cleaned, or rebuilt later.

---

sections.heading: Fix the Leak Before Fresh Insulation Goes In
sections.markdown:
Water can enter around shingles, flashing, roof valleys, vents, chimneys, skylights, and other penetrations. Once inside, it may travel along decking or framing before reaching the insulation, so the stain below does not always show the full path.

The roofer should correct the source and address damaged roofing or decking. The attic should then be inspected to determine whether the insulation can remain or whether it needs to be removed.

A small damp area discovered quickly may have a different answer than insulation that is soaked, matted, smelly, or damaged. Fresh insulation should not be installed until the leak is repaired and the attic is ready.

For a detailed moisture decision, see [Wet Attic Insulation: Can It Dry, or Does It Need to Be Removed?](https://goodattic.energy/resources/wet-attic-insulation-remove-or-dry/).

---

sections.heading: A New Roof Is a Good Time to Look for the Openings Pests Used
sections.markdown:
Mice, bats, squirrels, birds, and other animals often enter near the same parts of the home a roofing crew is already examining: vents, roofline gaps, soffits, fascia, chimneys, flashing transitions, and utility penetrations.

Replacing the roof alone does not automatically close every pest opening. Some gaps may be part of the roof or trim work. Others may require wildlife exclusion, pest control, siding repair, screening, or attic-focused entry-point work.

Handle active mice or wildlife first. If the insulation has been contaminated, covering the problem during the roof project will not solve it. The attic should be remediated before fresh insulation is installed.

Related guides:

- [Does Attic Insulation Need to Be Removed After Mice?](https://goodattic.energy/resources/attic-insulation-removal-after-mice/)
- [What Should Happen When Bat Guano Reaches Attic Insulation?](https://goodattic.energy/resources/bat-guano-attic-insulation-removal/)

---

sections.heading: Roofing and Attic Restoration Are Connected, but They Are Not the Same Job
sections.markdown:
### The roofer may handle

- Shingles or other roofing material
- Underlayment and flashing
- Roof decking repairs
- The roof leak itself
- Roof-mounted vents and penetrations
- Fascia or soffit repairs when included in the roofing project

### The attic contractor may handle

- Inspecting the existing insulation
- Removing wet, damaged, or contaminated insulation
- Cleaning and preparing the attic
- Attic-floor air sealing
- Baffles and ventilation preparation
- Attic-focused pest entry work
- Installing fresh blown-in insulation
- Progress and completion photos

### Another professional may handle

- Active bat or wildlife exclusion
- Plumbing or HVAC problems
- Electrical or structural repairs
- Mold evaluation or water-remediation work
- Suspected asbestos or vermiculite

Make sure each contractor’s quote clearly explains who is responsible for every part of the project. Clear responsibility keeps important work from being assumed, duplicated, or missed.

---

sections.heading: The Roofer and Attic Contractor Should Agree on the Plan Before Either Project Begins
sections.markdown:
The best order depends on what the inspection finds.

### A practical sequence

1. **Inspect the roof and attic.** Identify leaks, damaged decking, wet insulation, pest activity, air-sealing needs, and ventilation concerns.
2. **Handle active pests and specialist issues.** Wildlife exclusion, electrical repairs, hazardous materials, or structural concerns may need to come first.
3. **Remove damaged insulation when early access is helpful.** This can expose the attic floor, decking, and entry points before the roofing or attic work is completed.
4. **Complete the roofing work.** Repair the leak, replace damaged decking, and finish the roof-related vents, flashing, soffit, or fascia work.
5. **Prepare the attic.** Complete the cleanup, air sealing, baffles, ventilation preparation, and entry-point work in the agreed order.
6. **Install the final insulation layer.** Fresh insulation goes in after the attic is dry, repaired, and ready.

Some projects will use a different order. The important thing is that the roofer and attic contractor communicate before one crew covers an area the other still needs to reach.

---

### Why coordination helps

A shared plan can prevent one crew from covering an area the other still needs to reach. It also creates a chance to trace leaks, address pest openings, protect soffit airflow, and complete air sealing before the final insulation layer goes in.

This does not mean every new roof needs a full attic project. It means the attic is worth looking at while the timing is especially useful.

---

sections.markdown:
Good Attic can inspect the existing insulation, remove damaged or contaminated material, clean and prepare the space, complete the needed attic work, and install fresh blown-in cellulose when the attic is ready.

When another trade is needed, Good Attic can work alongside the roofer, wildlife professional, plumber, HVAC contractor, electrician, mold professional, structural professional, or other specialist so the work happens in the right order.

Good Attic builds the attic quote onsite and explains what can remain, what should come out, and which parts of the project belong to another professional. That helps the homeowner move forward with a coordinated plan rather than discovering the next problem after the roof is already finished.
